title: We Are Always Walking Each Other Home
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing our interconnectedness and letting go of control in order to find true fulfillment. They encourage us to appreciate the intricate web of relationships that shape our lives, from the simplest things like a candle or breakfast to the world around us, and to cultivate compassion and understanding for all beings and the natural world. By recognizing our dependence on others and the environment, we can shift our focus from the destination to the journey itself and find meaning in the unknown. This approach allows us to walk alongside one another, supporting each other home, and finding a sense of home within ourselves and with others.
topics: "we are always walking each other home"

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas, having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept.
I vow to taste the truth of the [unclear: "tatakara's"] words.*
Good morning.
It is so nice to see you here.
Frankly, I am surprised that so many of you showed up.
This weekend was and is so busy with different dharma activities.
The [unclear: "Lun Lake"] is about to start, and yesterday there was a Lei Entrustment Ceremony for Hegaku Balanced Peak, Talus Latona.
For that occasion, we met in person as a group inside a building for the first time since March 2020.
Sitting together after such a long time apart was a treat already.
The chanting of many voices was beautiful.
Our Doan Ryo and Tenkan supported us in the ceremonies.
It was really, really wonderful.
The questions and answers were wonderful too.
The questions were sincere and deep, and Talus answered them from the heart.
It was a true heart-to-heart meeting in and through ceremony.
Sangha meeting sangha, Buddha meeting Buddha, self meeting self.
Empowerments are part of the Soto Zen tradition.
Talus always said that it goes from heart to heart, and from warm hand to warm hand.
And then today we have a fundraiser.
Telephone, how should I put it, part of the fundraising campaign is that we are going to have a telephonic fundraiser this afternoon.
It was actually Tim's turn today, but he's going to be part of that, and we don't want him to burn out.
We are hoping to raise money for a down payment on the Zendo.
I am very grateful to all who have pitched in, and progress on that has been beautiful.
It appears that maybe house hunting and acquisition, or maybe buying land, building, or maybe remodeling something that already is built are the next steps in our journey home.
We are now in fall of 2021, and it's been quite a while to have had these face-to-face meetings.
I am very grateful to the Shambhala Center that let us use their beautiful facility in Bellingham.
It was so lovely to sit in that space and to be together.
Today is a perfect Pacific Northwest fall day.
It's cold, it's rainy, and the wind where I am and the rain are kind of coming sideways.
It rattles the building a bit, so you might be hearing some banging around when tree branches smack into the house.
On days like these, I am always concerned with losing power, or losing the Internet, or both.
For that reason, I usually send a copy of my Dharma talk to Thales.
But I didn't do that this time because I'm really concerned he wouldn't say all the nice things I want to tell you about him, about the sincerity and depth of his practice.
The joy of teaching was him and the privilege to have him as a friend.
So thank you very much, Thales, for taking on the responsibility of lay entrustment and deep bows to you.
Much gratitude.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Please don't be too embarrassed, because that's what Sangha friends and Dharma friends say about each other.
It's wonderful.
When I sit, sometimes a phrase comes to visit quite frequently.
I want to tell you about one that has been visiting me quite frequently.
The phrase is, "We are always walking each other home."
We are always walking each other home.
I don't remember where I heard it, or who said it.
Maybe that is not so important.
I know I could put it in a search engine, and I'm sure Google will find out all about it.
Maybe it'll point me to the person who said it, or it says 1,356,785 results.
Overwhelmed by variations and possibilities.
Yeah.
But I haven't done that, because it doesn't matter so much.
Sitting with this phrase, it has taken on its own meaning for me, for this one right here.
To me, it means being together.
It means having a home.
It means making an effort to assure safety and companionship.
It means Sangha.
It means that people walk me home.
And I'm grateful for it.
Sometimes the road is a little bumpy.
Sometimes it's a climb straight uphill.
And sometimes it's walking on a beautiful garden path.
Maybe I am reading too much into a simple sentence, but I don't think so.
My teacher, Norman Fischer, in the book Sailing Home, wrote the following.
*This leaving and having to return again and again is the constant shape of human consciousness.
Return is also a fact of nature.
The universe expands and contracts.
The tides go out and come in.
Celestial bodies go around and around.
The seasons begin, endure, draw to a close, come around again.*
*The spiritual journey, the human journey, is as natural as this.
We begin at home.
We leave home.
We return home.
Even when it looks like we are going far afield, we are always on our way back.
We have what we need and we are where we are going.
The spiritual journey is a journey of return.*
So when we leave home, we have ideas of what home is and we have ideas of what the journey is going to be.
We have ideas of what we will do once we leave and what it will look like.
What will we look for?
What will we find?
If I think of my own life, my own experience, I confess that I did not truly know the home I left.
I also confess that mostly my dreams and thoughts about the journey and the results were pretty far away from reality.
And I'm actually very happy that it is so.
I realize now that if my journey had happened the way I had envisioned, it would not have been this rich.
There would have been no surprises.
I think it would be terrible to actually know the future.
And yet it was a journey I needed to undertake.
Of course, now I am much older and not much wiser.
I understand a little, sometimes at least.
Friends, there is no map for this journey.
Even if we did have a map, what does the line on the paper have to do with sore feet, tripping down and falling down, and the courage to go on or maybe the decision not to go on?
Because we do need to leave, you see, so that later on we can find our way home again.
The trip we think we are on has actually very little to do with what our lives really are about.
The territory I covered while I was striving to reach a goal ended up forming my life so much more than the goal itself.
Has this ever happened to you?
Has it ever happened to you that you've worked for years toward an accomplishment?
You never quite make it, and it frustrates you, and you have desire and longing for that goal.
At a later time, you have that accomplishment, and it happens quite naturally, maybe because of the groundwork you laid for years, or maybe quite by accident.
And you may discover that that dream, that accomplishment, is no longer important, and maybe that it never was.
In a society that mostly judges and values people by their accomplishments, their achievements, one gets tossed about quite easily.
Taxes, jobs, for some even the up and down of the stock market, gas prices, success, failure: is this the journey we truly value in the end?
The story we plan, the story we want to tell, the story we want to shape, the story we want to control and present, the narrative.
So it will end according to our preference.
It's quite a thing.
And all the while, parallel, sometimes unnoticed, sometimes like a small wallflower, sometimes like an underground fungus, huge, old, and mysterious, is our spiritual journey.
Like I said, there is no map, no matter what other people draw in front of us and direct us to go toward.
Part of the spiritual journey, the spiritual narrative, is given to us at birth.
Race, color, privilege, socioeconomic status, religion.
We are given a lot of karma the moment we are born.
Sometimes we see it, and at times it is simply the background against which everything else shows up.
Some people are really curious about the spiritual journey.
Maybe we love the religion or lack thereof that we grew up with.
Or maybe we become seekers and connect with another tradition.
And some people really dip into many different religions.
Other delusions we carry with us is that we have a lot of control over our journey, that we are independent.
"Yes, I did this by myself."
We don't even need to look at something we might think is uncomplicated.
Let's look at this lovely little candle burning next to me.
It was given to me by a friend who made it.
And it was given to me by many, many bees who made this sweet smelling wax.
They could not have done that without flowers.
And the flowers wouldn't bloom unless there was soil to grow in, the right nutrients, sunshine and rain.
Or let's look at a simple breakfast.
Oatmeal and some fruit on top, and some soy yogurt.
How many hands touched my breakfast?
Someone grew the oats and the berries and the soybeans.
Someone harvested, someone processed, someone packaged and packed.
Someone brought it to the grocery store.
Someone [unclear: "stuck"] the shelves.
Someone turned on the lights.
All done by hands and minds.
Truckers, clerks, farmers.
Heck, someone had to build the roads used to transport the goods.
And someone had to build the trucks and the grocery store.
Together, only together.
Only a Buddha and the Buddha can do all this.
Held rightly, we should celebrate the incredible work that went into this breakfast.
Or we should weep, overwhelmed by how much it took to satisfy this small hunger, to provide nourishment for one meal.
We should be on our knees in gratitude to the earth, the sun, the rain, the animal lives, the human lives, the joy and the sorrow.
Always walking each other home.
Dependence, independence, interdependence.
The closer I look, the harder it becomes to find the dividing line.
And the harder it is to know who is walking whom home.
The wonderful Mary Oliver wrote a poem about the journey, and I would like to share it with you.
Mary Oliver, The Journey.
*One day, you finally knew that you had to and began, though the voices around you kept shouting their bad advice, though the whole house began to tremble and you felt the old tug at your ankles.*
*[unclear: "Meant"] my life, each voice cried.
But you didn't stop.
You knew what you had to do, though the wind pried with its stiff fingers at the very foundations.
Though the melancholy was terrible, it was already late enough in the wild night and the road full of fallen branches and stones.
Little by little, as you left the voice behind, the stars began to burn through the sheets of clouds.
And there was a new voice, which you slowly recognized as your own, that kept you company as you strode deeper and deeper into the world.
Determined to do the only thing you could do.
Determined to save the only life you could save.*
Thank you very much for listening to this talk.
If you find something useful, or you recognize yourself, please take it to heart.
If this talk was not useful to you, I would like to sincerely ask you to forget every word and to please just continue with your practice.
May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
